newsitem.title: USA: Gore, Gephardt curry favor of labor unionists.
newsitem.headline: Gore, Gephardt curry favor of labor unionists.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore and House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt, who may be rivals for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2000, Wednesday addressed labour union activists in an early bid for favour.

Addressing the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME), Gore and Gephardt both presented themselves as die-hard supporters of organised labour. They used many of the same arguments and occasionally identical words.

Both thanked labour unionists for their support in the 1996 election, both pledged to stop Republican efforts to limit labour rights, both took credit for last year's increase in the minimum wage and both promised to help narrow the gap between rich and poor.
"President Clinton and I will do everything possible to hold back a Congress that still seems determined to roll back worker protections," said Gore.
"You're not ever going to see a proposal that undermines labour principles get past this White House. It's not going to happen," he said.
Said Gephardt, who spoke an hour after Gore had left the conference room: "We have to have a set of policies in this country that help real people make it."
He denounced the welfare reform bill signed by Clinton with Gore's support last year as a "cruel hoax" perpetrated against poor people.

Gore enters the contest for the Democratic presidential nomination for 2000 as the front-runner. A poll this week gave him the support of 44 percent of Democratic voters, ahead of civil rights leader Jesse Jackson with 12 percent. Gephardt was in fourth place with six percent.
But Gore's aura of invincibility has dissipated because of his alleged involvement in questionable Democratic fundraising.

Gephardt, who seems eager to challenge Gore, has recently been visiting strategic states such as Iowa and New Hampshire where the first big votes of the presidential race will take place. He has also hired political advisers with important links to labour unions.
Although Gore is well regarded by labour leaders, who remain an important constituency in the Demeocratic Party, many unionists regard Gephardt as one of their own.

This was reflected in the introductions Gore and Gephardt received Wednesday from AFSCME president Gerald McEntee who called Gore a friend but gave Gephardt a much more effusive and heartfelt welcome.

"You don't even have to pick up the phone and tell him (Gephardt) what your position is because inevitably ... that politician is on the same page as you. He's a friend, an ally and a supporter because he believes in the same issues and solutions as we believe in," said McEntee.
Some unionists still blame Gore for his support for the North American Free Trade Agreement, which Gephardt opposed.
Both Gore and Gephardt showed off their union pedigrees. Gore said his father was the first secretary of labour in Tennesse and "implemented the very first labour laws in our part of the country."
Gephardt said his father was a milk truck driver in St Louis and a proud member of the Teamsters union.
